title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The core failure here is a data-sourcing decision made before deployment: the training pipeline ingested copyrighted recordings at scale, apparently without licenses, and the resulting models can reproduce recognizable melodic and rhythmic elements from those recordings. This is a failure at the data-collection and model-training stage, not at inference time alone. The outputs then made the underlying training practice visible, because plaintiffs could reconstruct near-matches to specific well-known songs simply by describing genre, era, and artist style in a prompt.

A catch at the data-curation stage would have required either licensing agreements before training began, or filtering mechanisms capable of excluding copyrighted material. Neither appears to have been in place. The admission that training used essentially all music files on the internet, and the subsequent discovery through a hack that sources included YouTube, Deezer, and Genius, indicate no meaningful rights-clearance process was applied. The gap between what the systems can produce and what their developers were licensed to use for training is what the litigation turns on.

What is not established is intent: lawsuits and court rulings in one jurisdiction are not findings of fact in others, settlements are not admissions of liability, and the allegation of deliberate concealment of training data has not been adjudicated in all pending proceedings.

summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse both companies of illegally copying thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their artificial intelligence systems. The lawsuits allege that the companies have deliberately hidden which songs they used and claim this represents copyright infringement on a massive scale. The record labels submitted evidence showing they were able to recreate famous songs by using specific prompts with the AI generators, demonstrating the systems directly reproduce sections of well-known music from artists like The Beatles, The Beach Boys, Michael Jackson, and many others.

To build their cases, the record labels used the AI music generators with targeted prompts describing song characteristics like release decade, genre, and artist style, then compared the outputs to original recordings they own. They documented numerous examples of AI-generated songs that replicate the distinctive melodies and rhythms of copyrighted material. The companies have previously claimed their training on copyrighted material qualifies as fair use, but the lawsuits reject this defense. These cases represent a major legal battle over how generative AI services should operate regarding copyrighted content across music, art, video, and text.
